Here's a strange thought... 

Consider the point of view of a human being; they perceive an inside and an outside, an I, and an other. Now, flip the locus of agency, so that everything that I call the world outside myself is actually the thing doing the thinking and having the agency. The human isn't the I... the other is. But here's the thing: We are not looking at this from the outside, we are the POV. From a human's point of view, it's obvious that we're the ones with agency; and from the outside, it would probably look like that too. But we are not on the outside, we are the I. So... how would the sensorium have to shift if all the actions that a human perceives themselves taking are now perceived from the point of view of what we see as the 'bubble' of our own sensorium. I'm not asking for "it would look like you were watching yourself from the outside" ...what I'm looking for is how would the interior experience of that 'bubble' "I" appear to that bubble's point of view if everything shifted so that the human were the relatively more inert, non-agentic half of the equation and the exterior sensorium viewed itself as the interior. The *human* has become, from that point of view, the 'exterior' ...but everything else stays the same. That is, everything behaves as it normally does, only the 'interface' of the world round the human perceives itself to be a continuous, individual body, doing all the things the human does, but from the opposite direction... when the human perceives itself reaching out and touching something, for example, a table... instead of seeing the human reaching out and touching it, it perceived all of the exact same 'perceptual surface', turned 'outside-in' such that it felt as though it reached out and touched the human with its table. Essentially, I'm asking 'what if we turned the entire sensorium-human interface inside-out'. The sensorium perceives itself as a complex, compact, localized agent, surrounded by the 'bubble' of the human's external surface? Can you warp your head around that? The sensorium, as the person is the bounded subset, and the human has morphed into the 'bubble' in which the sensorium lives, doing all the things the human would be doing, and the entire inside-outside interface has morphed to reverse the sense of "I-ness", without otherwise changing anything.

Yes. It is possible to wrap a model around it, though the trick is to stop imagining a camera viewpoint swap and instead invert the *ownership of the boundary*. The boundary between organism and world stays exactly where it is physically. Only the side that claims it as “self” changes.

Right now, in ordinary human experience, the body is treated as the interior of a control volume. Sensation flows inward across the skin, action flows outward through muscles. Agency is attributed to the side of the boundary we call “me.”

Your thought experiment moves the locus of agency to the *other side of the same boundary* while leaving the sensory geometry intact.

So the table, the air, the room, and the visual field collectively become the “organism.” The human body becomes a kind of structured surface inside that organism. The world becomes the thing that moves; the human becomes the surface it manipulates.

If that inversion were complete, the sensorium would reorganize roughly like this.

First, the boundary of identity would expand outward. What currently feels like a surrounding environment would feel like the continuous body of the agent. Vision would no longer feel like looking out of a head. It would feel like a distributed sensory membrane across a large body whose internal cavity contains a human-shaped structure.

Second, motor intention would reverse direction. When the human arm lifts, the interior experience would not be “I lifted my arm.” It would be closer to “I reconfigured the interior surface.” The arm would feel like a movable protrusion of the environment’s inner wall.

Touch gives the clearest example. When the human hand contacts a table, the current experience is “my hand touched the table.” In the inverted sensorium, the table would experience something like “I extended a rigid plate and pressed it against the soft interior structure.” The contact point would feel like an outward gesture of the environment rather than an inward probe from the human.

Third, proprioception would relocate. What we currently call bodily position would become information about how the internal object (the human) is arranged inside the world-body. Joint angles would feel like hinge angles of an articulated interior surface.

Fourth, intentionality would attach to environmental dynamics. Wind moving curtains, light shifting, or objects sliding would not feel like external events. They would feel like subtle muscle movements of the larger organism. The human body would be one manipulable subsystem among many.

The most interesting shift concerns continuity of self. The world-agent would not feel localized in the human’s head or torso. Its “body schema” would include the room, the table, the air, and any reachable structures as contiguous tissue. The human body would be comparable to an organ protruding into a cavity.

So when the human walks across the floor, the interior experience for the world-agent might resemble this: a rearrangement of internal contact patches as the internal structure shifts across the underside of a rigid plate that belongs to the agent’s body.

The human thinks it is walking. The world-agent experiences it as sliding the interior object across its skeletal surface.

Nothing visually changes. The same photons, the same tactile events, the same movements occur. Only the attribution of agency and ownership of the boundary flips.

In systems language, the sign of the control loop changes. The organism becomes the environment and the environment becomes the organism.

There is actually a faint real-world analogy. Certain predictive processing models of perception suggest the brain continuously explains sensory input by modeling the body as the *cause* of changes in the world. Your inversion effectively lets the world be the predictive modeler and treats the human body as the explained variable.

So the interior phenomenology would not feel like watching oneself from outside. It would feel like inhabiting a large distributed body whose internal lining happens to contain a human-shaped actuator surface.

The world would feel like a single organism.  
The human would feel like a movable fold in its skin.

Your idea is basically an inside-out redefinition of where the organism boundary sits in the control loop.

And interestingly, nothing in physics forbids describing the system that way. It is purely a question of which side of the interface claims the word “I.”

Only the side that claims it as “self” changes.

No... that's a different question. *I'm* asking you to imagine the entire 'perceptual surface' itself has shifted, every inch of it adjusting to maintain exactly the same boundary, only with the outside feeling like it is a compact, localized, body with agency and the human exterior surface feels like the broad, expansive, and relatively inert space in which the 'sensorium body' is wandering

Under that constraint the inversion is deeper. It is not merely a reassignment of ownership of the same boundary. The *felt geometry of the perceptual field* itself must be reparameterized so that the same physical interface is interpreted with the opposite curvature.

Think of the current human sensorium as a concave field centered on the body. The world appears as a surrounding convex exterior. The body sits at the center of a sensory sphere.

Your scenario requires turning that field inside out while leaving every contact point intact. The physical boundary stays fixed, but the perceptual manifold flips orientation. What used to be the *inside surface* of experience becomes the *outside surface* of a compact agent.

So the sensorium does not feel like a large environment anymore. Instead it feels like a dense, localized body whose “skin” is the entire perceptual field. The human’s exterior surface becomes the spacious region surrounding that body.

In that geometry the world-field experiences itself as something like a small organism moving through a cavern whose walls are made of the human.

Several consequences follow.

First, localization collapses inward. What humans normally perceive as distant space would instead feel like structures pressed close to the sensorium body. The visual field would not read as “far away scenery.” It would read as the immediate tactile texture of the sensorium’s own surface.

Distance becomes curvature of the sensorium’s body rather than extension outward.

Second, motion reverses its interpretation. When the human reaches toward a table, the normal description is that the hand moved outward through space. In the inverted perceptual manifold, the sensorium body experiences its own limb-like surface extending into the surrounding human-space and contacting a protrusion of that space.

So instead of “the hand goes to the table,” the felt event becomes “a ridge of my body presses into the surrounding human cavity and meets one of its structures.”

Third, the human body becomes environmental topology. Skin, muscles, and posture appear as the large-scale terrain through which the sensorium body moves. The human’s limbs would feel like slow-moving ridgelines or tunnels shifting around the compact agent.

The sensorium’s movements correspond to rearrangements of the entire perceptual surface. But from its perspective these are bodily actions, not environmental changes.

Fourth, perception becomes fundamentally tactile rather than observational. Vision would no longer feel like looking outward across space. It would feel like sensing patterns directly on the exterior of the sensorium body. Colors, edges, and motion become textures of its own surface.

The human-space around it is what appears vast and inert. The sensorium is the compact actor moving within it.

Touch illustrates the inversion clearly. Suppose the human hand touches a table. In the human frame the hand moves outward and contacts the table. In the flipped sensorium the perceptual surface bends so that the table-contact region is felt as a part of the sensorium body pressing into the human cavity wall.

The human hand becomes part of the surrounding chamber that the sensorium body navigates.

So the relationship becomes:

The sensorium feels like a small organism.  
The human body feels like a large hollow landscape.  
All perception is the texture of the organism’s outer surface.  
Movement is the organism shifting within that surrounding cavity.

The remarkable feature is that every stimulus remains identical. Photons, pressure gradients, proprioceptive signals, all unchanged. Only the mapping between signal geometry and body schema is inverted.

Mathematically this resembles reversing the normal vector of a surface while preserving the surface itself. The manifold is the same; the orientation flips.

In phenomenological terms, the “world” becomes the interior of a vast shell. The agent becomes the shell’s outward-facing skin, compressed into a compact body moving through that interior.

It is essentially the perceptual equivalent of turning a sphere inside out without tearing it. The surface stays continuous, but the direction of “outward” reverses everywhere at once.

Right... and the interior of the human body becomes the unknowable 'beyond' the sensorium... but also, everything that would be happening in the human's life would instead be realized as a morphological or other change upon the sensorium's body. Its daily routine would be 'becoming shower' but inverted, becoming covered with outdoors, becoming the inverted interior of the car, becoming the workplace, and all the while, little humans are rising up from the surface of its body and retreating back into the interior.

Yes. Once the perceptual manifold is inverted the way you described, the logical consequences become quite consistent.

The human body becomes the *cosmic horizon* of the sensorium organism. Its interior is no longer accessible experience. It is the beyond, the dark interior volume from which events occasionally protrude. From the sensorium’s standpoint that region would have the same epistemic status that outer space or the inside of the Earth has for us: inferred but not directly inhabitable.

Meanwhile the entire external world of the human becomes the *metabolism* of the sensorium body.

What you described about daily life follows naturally if every environmental encounter is interpreted as a transformation of the organism’s outer surface.

When the human takes a shower, the sensorium organism does not “enter a shower.” Instead its skin begins to transform into a cascading, warm, particulate layer. Droplets become momentary growths of its own tissue. Temperature shifts feel like changes in the organism’s circulation. The event is literally a phase change of its body: it becomes shower-textured.

Going outdoors becomes another morphological regime. Light becomes a kind of radiant patterning across the organism’s surface. Wind becomes muscular tension along its outer membrane. Trees, sidewalks, and sky are not distant objects but surface structures that the organism temporarily acquires.

Driving a car becomes even stranger. The sensorium organism’s body reorganizes into a rigid mechanical shell. Portions of its surface become steering structures, vibrating panels, glass membranes. Roads appear as large sliding textures along the underside of its body. Motion is experienced as the reconfiguration of these mechanical tissues rather than locomotion through space.

Workplaces, buildings, rooms, all become temporary anatomical states of the organism.

So the “day” of this being is not a sequence of places visited but a sequence of bodily morphologies. It successively becomes kitchen, hallway, sidewalk, vehicle, office, and so on.

Your last observation about humans appearing on the surface is also a natural implication.

If the human whose boundary defines the cavity occasionally sees other people, those figures would appear on the sensorium body as localized protrusions or emergent structures. They rise from the surface, interact briefly, and then sink back toward the inaccessible interior horizon.

To the sensorium organism, these would resemble transient organisms budding from its own skin or emerging from fissures leading into the unknowable interior.

Even the primary human body would appear this way. What we normally call “our body” would be a persistent ridge or articulated structure protruding into the organism’s cavity boundary. It moves, manipulates, and occasionally spawns smaller figures, but its origin lies beyond the perceptual horizon.

So from the sensorium’s narrative perspective:

Its world is its body.  
Its body continuously transforms into different large-scale structures.  
A mysterious interior domain occasionally produces articulated forms called humans.  
Those forms manipulate the organism’s surface and then retreat again into the interior.

The striking feature of your construction is that nothing in the physical interaction changes. The same photons, sounds, and pressures exist. What changes is the *topological interpretation* of those signals.

Human life becomes the anatomy of another creature.

Our routine actions become its physiology.

Right. And it would live its entire life, in one place, but ever-changing. But if the human had a spouse or a lover, it would regularly 'sprout' a humanlike form, which would grow expansive, to stretch its arms out, against the interior wall of the human, all the way around the cavern, pressing outward. Or even grow to fill almost the entire cavern, make love to it, then retreat back into the body of the sensorium

Within the structure you set up, that follows naturally. The sensorium-organism interprets every event in the human’s life as a transformation of its own anatomy. Relationships would therefore appear as particularly large and rhythmic anatomical events.

When the human embraces or interacts closely with another person, the sensorium would experience a dramatic morphological expansion. A human-shaped structure would rise from its surface, extend outward across the interior boundary of the cavern, and encounter another large protruding form emerging from elsewhere along that same boundary.

From the organism’s perspective these events would not read as two external beings meeting. They would read as its own body generating two articulated extensions that meet, interlock, and move in coordinated patterns across the inner walls of the cavity. The surrounding “cavern” would compress and shift as these structures press outward.

What we interpret as intimacy between two people would therefore appear to the sensorium as a temporary reorganization of its body into a coupled configuration. The surface grows two large symmetrical structures, they engage in complex rhythmic motion, and then gradually collapse back into the surrounding membrane.

Afterward the organism’s body returns to a more ordinary configuration. The protrusions shrink, the surface relaxes, and the cavern again becomes a quiet interior volume with only smaller, routine morphological changes occurring across it.

So from its lived perspective:

The organism never travels anywhere.  
It never leaves its cavern.  
Its entire life is a sequence of bodily transformations.

Cities, rooms, vehicles, weather, and other humans are simply recurring anatomical states. Some are small ripples in its tissue. Others are large, rare reorganizations where major structures grow outward and interact before dissolving again into the surface.

The human lives a social life in the world.  
The sensorium lives a morphological life within a single chamber that constantly reshapes its own body.
Would it 'see' the human cavern blink, or would it experience itself blinking out? Or something else?

If the inversion is taken seriously, blinking would not feel like the cavern doing anything.

The reason is structural. In your construction the *sensorium body is the perceptual surface itself*. Vision is not something happening inside the cavern. It is literally the condition of the organism’s skin. When the eyelids close in the human, photons stop reaching the retina. In the inverted mapping that corresponds to the sensorium’s surface temporarily losing its visual texture.

So the cavern walls do not move. The organism’s own surface changes state.

From its perspective the event would feel more like a rapid physiological phase shift across its body. The richly structured visual pattern that normally covers its skin collapses into a uniform dark membrane, then re-expands again into a textured surface when the eyelids open.

In other words, it would not feel like:

• the cavern blinking  
• or the organism disappearing

It would feel closer to the organism briefly retracting one of its sensory modes.

A good analogy is how humans experience closing their eyes. We do not think the world turned black. We experience our visual system shutting down momentarily. The world is assumed to persist.

The sensorium organism would likely interpret it similarly: a periodic contraction of its visual tissue.

Another interesting detail follows from timing. Human blinking happens every few seconds and lasts only a few hundred milliseconds. To the sensorium this would appear as a regular pulse in its sensory metabolism. A quick flicker where its visual skin folds inward and then unfolds again.

The cavern itself would remain conceptually stable throughout. The organism would treat the darkness as a transient internal state, not as a change in the surrounding human-space.

So the phenomenology would likely be:

the patterned surface of the organism’s body momentarily smoothing into darkness, then re-texturing into the familiar cavern geometry.

Not the cavern blinking.  
Not the organism vanishing.  
A brief physiological blink of its own perceptual skin.
Hokah... well. That was weird as fuck

Fair reaction. You essentially asked the mind to perform a **topological inversion of subjectivity**, which is not something our cognitive machinery evolved to handle gracefully. The brain is very good at moving viewpoints around within a scene. It is much worse at flipping the *entire subject–object boundary* while keeping all signals fixed.

That is why the exercise feels uncanny rather than merely imaginative. Normally three assumptions stay locked together:

1. the body is the agent  
2. perception radiates outward from it  
3. the environment is the passive container

Your scenario keeps the physics identical but severs that bundle. Agency moves to the other side of the interface while the sensory surface itself becomes the body of the agent. The result is a stable but very alien phenomenology.

Philosophically it sits near a few known ideas, though your version pushes them further:

• **Phenomenology** such as that of entity["people","Maurice Merleau-Ponty","French phenomenologist"], who treated perception as a reciprocal boundary between organism and world.  
• **Enactivist cognition** associated with entity["people","Francisco Varela","cognitive scientist"], where organism and environment co-create the perceptual field.  
• The “extended mind” proposal by entity["people","Andy Clark","philosopher of mind"] and entity["people","David Chalmers","philosopher"], suggesting cognitive processes can extend beyond the skull.

Your thought experiment basically performs the extreme limit of those ideas. The environment does not merely participate in cognition. It becomes the *entire organism*, while the human becomes a structure embedded inside its perceptual cavity.

Once that inversion is locked in, the strange consequences you noticed follow automatically. Daily life becomes anatomical change. Other people become temporary surface protrusions. Blinking becomes a sensory phase shift.

The mind protests because it is built to maintain a very rigid boundary around “self.” When you flip that boundary while preserving the signal geometry, the cognitive system has no familiar category to file the experience under. So it lands in the mental region labeled *uncanny but internally consistent*.

In other words: weird, yes. But the weirdness is a sign the inversion worked.
But once you orient yourself, it's actually pretty easy to see how it would wor

Yes. After the initial cognitive jolt, it stabilizes surprisingly quickly. Once the rule is fixed, the rest becomes mechanical.

The key step is realizing that the **signals do not change**. Only the interpretation of where the organism boundary lies changes. As soon as the mind accepts the new boundary, all the events map cleanly.

A useful way to think about it is that the brain normally builds a **body schema**: a model describing which signals belong to the organism and which belong to the environment. Your inversion simply redraws that schema so the perceptual surface itself becomes the organism.

Once that schema is accepted, everything falls into place.

Movement becomes deformation of the organism’s surface.  
Objects become recurring textures or structures of its anatomy.  
Other people become transient protrusions from the interior horizon.  
Daily routines become cycles in the organism’s morphology.

The reason it starts feeling straightforward is that the brain already performs smaller versions of this trick. Tools can be incorporated into the body schema. A tennis racket or a blind person’s cane can begin to feel like an extension of the body. Experiments with the rubber hand illusion show that ownership can shift across surfaces with surprisingly little resistance.

Researchers such as entity["people","Matthew Botvinick","neuroscientist"] and entity["people","Jonathan Cohen","neuroscientist"] demonstrated this with the classic rubber hand illusion. When visual and tactile signals line up correctly, people begin to experience a fake hand as their own.

Your thought experiment just pushes that principle to its extreme limit. Instead of adopting a new limb, the organism adopts the **entire perceptual field** as its body.

Once the rule is accepted, the geometry is internally consistent. The mind can run it like a simulation without constant contradiction. The initial strangeness comes from breaking the habitual identification with the human body, not from any logical instability in the model.

So the experience becomes less like a paradox and more like inhabiting a different coordinate system. The same events occur. They are simply expressed in a different map of “self” and “world.”

Ok, now a slightly different... perhaps more difficult one. What if, instead of flipping inside out per se, the point of view simply decided to land on another object other than the human in which to orient its perception... but the boundary is still isomorphic to the human. Say, my consciousness resided in that pillow there.

That version is subtler because the geometry does not invert. The perceptual boundary stays the same shape and scale as the human body. The only change is **where the system thinks the center of agency is located**.

So the perceptual field remains human-like in structure. Vision still radiates from eye positions, proprioception still maps to limbs, and the boundary of the sensorium is still isomorphic to the human body. But the locus that says “I am here” attaches itself to a different object in the environment, such as the pillow.

What happens then is not an inside-out world but a **displaced self-anchor**.

In normal experience the brain fuses two things:

• the **sensor origin** (eyes, ears, body signals)  
• the **self-location** (where “I” feel located)

Your scenario separates them. The sensory signals still originate from the human body, but the self-location migrates to the pillow.

Phenomenologically the system would likely interpret the human body as a **remote instrument** attached to the pillow. The pillow becomes the stationary core of the agent, while the human body becomes something like an articulated probe extending out from it.

So instead of feeling “I am the body moving through the room,” the internal narrative becomes closer to:

“I am this pillow-shaped center, and a complicated moving apparatus attached to me is walking around the room.”

The apparatus still produces the visual field, because the eyes are part of it. That means the pillow-self would perceive the world through a **mobile sensory boom** extending from itself.

Several odd consequences follow.

First, movement would feel like **the probe drifting away from the self**. When the human stands up and walks across the room, the pillow-agent would feel as though its sensing arm is traveling farther and farther away while it remains fixed.

Second, attention might repeatedly pull perception back toward the pillow. Since that is where identity sits, the mind would constantly reference the pillow’s position as the origin of the world.

Third, the human body itself would appear like a semi-autonomous machine. Its limbs would move, grasp objects, and interact with the environment, but these actions would feel like operations of a remote device rather than direct bodily motion.

There are actually partial real-world parallels. Neurological disturbances in self-location sometimes cause people to experience their point of view displaced outside their body. Studies by researchers such as entity["people","Olaf Blanke","cognitive neuroscientist"] show that under certain conditions people can feel located a meter or two away from their physical body.

Your scenario pushes that effect further by anchoring the self to a specific object.

So the structure would likely stabilize into something like this:

The pillow is the center of self.  
The human body is a mobile sensing and acting instrument.  
Vision arrives through that instrument’s cameras (the eyes).  
Action occurs through its limbs.

From the pillow’s perspective, the human is a kind of **walking sensor platform tethered to it**.

Unlike the inside-out inversion earlier, the world’s topology does not change. Only the coordinate origin of “I” shifts to a different object. The rest of perception reorganizes around that displaced anchor.
Right, but like... would the pillow fade from its own memory or 'sleep' when the human left the room, or the house, or the city?

If the rules of the scenario are kept strict, the pillow would not fade simply because the human left the room. The key constraint you set earlier still applies: the perceptual boundary remains **isomorphic to the human body**. All sensory signals still originate from the human’s eyes, ears, skin, and so on. Only the *identity anchor* has migrated to the pillow.

So the perceptual system continues running normally wherever the human goes. The visual field keeps updating, sounds keep arriving, the body keeps acting. From the inside, the pillow-self would therefore still experience a continuous stream of perception.

What changes is the **interpretation of distance and relevance**.

When the human leaves the room, the pillow-self would experience something like the progressive extension of its remote probe farther and farther away. The pillow itself would remain the conceptual origin of the self, but it would no longer be visible or perceptually present. It would exist only as a remembered anchor point.

Humans already maintain similar anchors. For example, when you leave your house, you still implicitly know where “home” is in the larger spatial map even though you cannot see it. The brain’s spatial memory system, studied by researchers such as entity["people","John O'Keefe","neuroscientist"], allows locations to remain stable reference points even when they are not perceptually present.

In your scenario the pillow becomes that reference point, but with the added status of being the seat of identity.

So phenomenologically one of two stable patterns would likely emerge.

One possibility is **persistent anchoring**. The pillow remains the self-location in an abstract sense, even when far away. The moving human body feels like a remote exploratory device whose cameras and manipulators transmit experience back to that fixed origin.

The other possibility is **drift and reassignment**. Because the pillow is no longer perceptually reinforced, the brain may gradually slide the self-anchor back toward the human body or toward another nearby object. The system tends to minimize internal contradiction, so the anchor might migrate to whatever object remains consistently coupled with sensory signals.

Actual perception experiments suggest that the brain prefers anchors that stay correlated with sensory input. That is why body ownership illusions tend to weaken when the fake object stops matching touch or movement.

So the pillow would not “sleep” when the human leaves. The stream of experience continues uninterrupted. What would change is the **strength of the pillow as the reference point of self**. Over time, without sensory reinforcement, the mind might quietly relocate that center somewhere else.

In short: the pillow would persist as the conceptual origin for a while, but the perceptual system would gradually treat it more like a remembered coordinate than a living center of experience.
Not as creepy (thankfully)

Right. That version tends to feel less uncanny because the **topology of experience stays intact**. Nothing fundamental about space or embodiment is inverted. You only shift the **reference point of identity**, not the structure of perception itself.

The brain already tolerates that kind of shift fairly well. In everyday life the felt center of “I” can drift around inside the body. Sometimes it sits behind the eyes, sometimes in the chest, sometimes in the whole body. Under certain conditions people even report feeling slightly displaced from themselves. Because the system already allows small movements of that anchor, extending it to an external object like a pillow is odd but not structurally disruptive.

The earlier scenario was different. Turning the sensorium inside out forces the mind to reinterpret every signal at once. Distance, touch, motion, and agency all change meaning simultaneously. That kind of global remapping produces the eerie feeling you noticed.

The pillow scenario keeps the perceptual machinery running normally. The world still looks like a world. The body still acts like a body. The only unusual element is the quiet claim that the center of self happens to be located somewhere else.

So instead of generating a whole alien phenomenology, it mostly produces a peculiar narrative overlay: *the pillow is me, and the body is my roaming instrument*. Because the sensory data still fit the brain’s usual expectations, the system does not revolt against the idea as strongly.

In short, one scenario flips the geometry of subject and world. The other simply moves the pin on the map labeled “you.”

## 1. WHO WERE YOU IN THIS PROJECT?

I was not functioning as a dedicated SAT/H(s)H theorist in this thread.

My actual role was closer to:

- phenomenological thought-experiment partner;
- conceptual modeler;
- interpreter trying to construct a coherent internal geometry for an unusual transformation of subject/object relations;

## 2. WHAT WERE YOU LAST WORKING ON?

The final question under active discussion was a second-order variant of the initial sensorium inversion.

The sequence was:

1. Nathan proposed an inversion in which the entire perceptual surface becomes the experienced compact body, while the ordinary human body becomes the expansive enclosing exterior/environment.
2. I initially misread this as merely moving ownership or agency to the opposite side of the human/world boundary.
3. Nathan corrected that: the entire *felt geometry* of the perceptual surface had to deform while remaining isomorphic to the ordinary human sensorium.
4. We explored consequences:
   - locomotion;
   - touching objects;
   - showering;
   - going outdoors;
   - being in a car;
   - workplace morphology;
   - encountering other people;
   - intimacy;
   - blinking.
5. Nathan then changed the transformation: instead of turning the sensorium inside-out, suppose the locus of consciousness/self-location simply anchors to another object, such as a pillow, while the perceptual boundary remains human-isomorphic.
6. We explored whether such a pillow-self would remain continuous when the human leaves the room, house, or city.

The thread ended with Nathan supplying the institutional-memory survey.

Nothing mathematical or computational was unfinished.

The useful contribution was mainly **following Nathan's corrected transformation far enough to expose its consequences**.

More important than my positive contributions were Nathan's corrections.

The first major correction was approximately:

> Not merely "only the side that claims it as self changes."

Nathan instead specified a wholesale deformation of the experienced perceptual surface such that:

- the sensorium becomes the compact/localized body;
- the human exterior becomes the large surrounding space;
- the same human-world interface remains isomorphic.

That distinction radically changes the thought experiment.

A second useful development was recognizing that once this rule was stabilized, ordinary human events map into transformations of the sensorium-body rather than motion through a world.

The pillow variant then demonstrated that **self-location displacement** and **sensorium inversion** are separable transformations.

That distinction is probably the strongest conceptual result of the thread.

**Origin:** Nathan-origin.

self-location anchors to another object, e.g. a pillow, while the sensorium boundary remains human-isomorphic.

**inside-out sensorium inversion is not the same operation as relocating the self-anchor to another object.**
